title: Riding backward
hook: he rides his donkey facing the tail, and every town tells a different reason why (Nasruddin tale)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nasruddin fed his soup to his fur coat, because the coat got the welcome he didn't. Your line was feed the person. Whose clothes did you catch yourself reading? Day thirty-eight.

Picture a dusty road in Anatolia, seven or eight hundred years ago. Here comes a man on a donkey, and something is wrong. He's sitting backward. His face is toward the donkey's tail, his back toward where he's going, and he is perfectly calm about it. People in the market stop and stare. A child laughs. Somebody finally calls out: Hoca, you're on your donkey the wrong way! And Nasruddin, the teacher nobody can decide is a fool or a sage, has an answer ready. The trouble is, every town that tells this story gives him a different answer. Today's story is riding backward.
screen: `A MAN ON A DONKEY.` → `FACING THE TAIL.` → `EVERY TOWN, A DIFFERENT REASON.`

segments.voice: Here's the answer told most often. Nasruddin is riding to the school with his students walking behind him. If I face forward, he says, my back is to you, and that's rude. If you walk in front of me, your backs are to me, and that's rude too. So I ride facing you, and we can all see each other. Problem solved. In another telling, he just wants to see where he's been. In another, the donkey knows the way, so why watch the road? And in some, there's no reason given at all. He rides backward, and the whole town argues about it. That's a clue to who Nasruddin is. The stories belong to Turkish, Persian and wider Muslim folk tradition, and they traveled far beyond it. Tradition places a real Nasreddin Hoca in thirteenth-century Anatolia, near the town of Akşehir, where a tomb bears his name. But hundreds of stories gathered around him over the centuries, and nobody can say which of them, if any, he really lived. Hoca, in Turkish, means teacher. So picture a teacher whose method is to do the ridiculous thing first and let you work out the lesson. And the lesson here is about direction. We ride through our days facing forward, eyes on the next thing, the next message, the next deadline. Nasruddin turns around. From the back of a donkey, the road you've already traveled is the whole view. You see who is walking with you. You see what you've passed. It isn't the wrong way. It's the other way, and it shows you what the front can't.
screen: `SO WE CAN SEE EACH OTHER.` · `ONE STORY, MANY ENDINGS.` · `HOCA MEANS TEACHER.` · `THE ROAD BEHIND IS THE VIEW.` · then, large: `NOT THE WRONG WAY. THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your day from the other end. Settle, and breathe. Start where you are, right now, and walk your day backward. What happened just before this? And before that? Keep going, one scene at a time, back toward the moment you woke up. Don't judge any of it. Just watch the road behind you, the way Nasruddin does from his donkey. Notice who was walking with you today. Notice one thing you passed without seeing. When you reach the morning, rest there. The bell holds the time.
Riding backward. Nasruddin on his donkey, facing the tail, so he can see the road behind him and the people walking with him. Today's word.
Your line: face the other way. Once today, when you're rushing toward the next thing, stop and turn around. Look back at what's already done, and at who's already beside you. Day thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Nasruddin stories are told aloud across Turkey, Iran, Central Asia, the Balkans and beyond, often by parents and teachers, and each telling may give its own ending; he is very often pictured riding his donkey backward.

notes: Nasruddin tales are oral and vary; the 'students walking behind' explanation is given as the most common telling. Confirm this is fair.
Historical Nasreddin Hoca: tradition places him in 13th-century Anatolia, with a tomb at Akşehir. Stated as tradition, not fact. Confirm.
Hoca (Turkish, from Persian khwaja) glossed as 'teacher'; pronunciation given as ho-JAH (Turkish c = j, stress usually final). Confirm.
Spelling: the voice uses Nasruddin (as in the outline) and Nasreddin Hoca for the Turkish form. A Keeper may prefer one spelling throughout.
